body.text: Craft night is one of the easiest ways to host. There's no cooking, no seating chart and no playlist panic, because busy hands do half the work of keeping conversation going. What you need is a craft that nobody can get badly wrong, a clear table and an end time.
Below: five craft menus to choose from, with what to set out for each, a short checklist, a two-hour run of show and fixes for the things that tend to wobble.
Pick the craft first

Projects that work well are quick, forgiving and charming even when wonky. Aim for something finished in about two hours that needs little explaining and no special equipment. With a mix of confident crafters and total beginners, skip fiddly techniques like sewing or sculpting unless you can demonstrate them.
1. Paint-your-own pottery or ceramics

Buy ready-made ceramic pieces and acrylic paints or a ceramic painting kit, and everyone paints a mug, dish or trinket. Cost depends on the piece. Treat painted pottery as display-only unless the kit or studio says it is food safe for your use. Read the paint labels too, look for the ACMI AP or CL seal, and avoid products containing lead, cadmium or other heavy metals. If your group would rather paint than craft, [how to host a paint night at home](/journal/how-to-host-a-paint-night-at-home) goes deeper on that one evening.

**What to set out:** a ceramic painting kit or ready-made pieces, a set of acrylic craft paints and {{product:benicci-12-piece-artist-paint-brush-set|a brush set}} to share, so every guest has a piece and a brush from the first minute.
2. Friendship bracelets and beads
Kits come with thread, beads and instructions, so you can start right away. Make one for yourself and one to swap. Check the label for small parts.
**What to set out:** a friendship bracelet kit for the table, so the thread, beads and instructions are all in one place and nobody waits for a turn with the beads.

body.title: Start with a kit made for groups
body.dek: Choose a project and the kit arrives together, so hosting is more about the fun than the shopping.

body.text: 3. Air-dry clay trinket dishes

Roll, press and smooth ([how to start air-dry clay](/journal/how-to-start-air-dry-clay) has more ideas). Everyone writes their name on a bit of paper and leaves their dish to dry; air-dry clay usually takes about 2 to 3 days, so check the label. It needs no kiln, and the results are decorative only, so keep food and drink off them, even if sealed.
**What to set out:** a bucket of air-dry clay, a small set of clay tools and a mat each, so rolling and cutting stay on the table and cleanup is a wipe.
4. Cookie decorating
Bake or buy plain sugar cookies, then set out icing, sprinkles and edible decorations. Ask about allergies when you invite people, and wash hands with soap and water before handling food.
**What to set out:** a cookie decorating kit with icing and sprinkles, plus a tray per guest, so everyone's cookies stay their own.
5. Collage or vision boards
Old magazines, scissors, glue sticks and a piece of card per guest. Good for friends who like to talk while they work.
**What to set out:** card, sharp scissors and {{product:scotch-glue-stick-photo-safe-4-pack|glue sticks}} for the table, so nobody waits for a turn with the glue.
Budget and invitations

Decide upfront whether you'll cover supplies, ask guests to chip in or have everyone bring something. What a night costs depends on the craft, the group size and where you shop. A quick message does it: 'I'll pick up supplies, could everyone chip in toward them?'

Keep the invitation short. Say what you're making, when it starts and ends, what to wear (nothing precious near paint) and whether to bring anything, and add 'no experience needed, wonky is welcome.' Ask about food allergies and dietary needs while you're at it. Send it about two weeks ahead and confirm a few days before.

essentials: A big table (or a few smaller ones) cleared of everything else
A paper or plastic tablecloth, or old newspapers
Supplies for each guest, plus a spare or two
Cups of water, paper towels and wet wipes for cleanup
Masking tape and a marker, for labeling drying projects
optional: Small trays for each guest's supplies
A snack table set away from the craft table
A phone for a group photo at the end
A small portable speaker for the playlist
A mini glue gun with a low-temperature setting, if a project needs a quick bond

body.text: A test run, a few days before

Make one practice version of the craft. Twenty minutes tells you how long it really takes, which step needs a demo, what you forgot to buy and whether the instructions make sense to a beginner. Keep the practice piece as the example, and say aloud on the night which step was fiddly for you. Guests relax when the host admits it.
The evening, minute by minute

items: 0:00 Welcome, drinks and snacks, music on low.
0:20 Show the craft. Do a quick demo, then let everyone start.
0:30 Free making time. Keep conversation going with a few easy questions.
1:45 Wrap up, show-and-tell, group photo. Everyone holds up what they made and names one thing they like about it.
2:00 Pack projects, label drying pieces, help with cleanup.

body.text: **What makes it easier:** a small portable speaker, so a playlist fills the room at a volume that still lets people talk.
When things wobble

items: **Someone says 'I'm not creative.'** Show them the simplest version and remind everyone that the point is the evening, not the result.
**Mixed skill levels.** Offer a basic version and a stretch version of the same project.
**Someone finishes early.** Keep extra supplies for a bonus project, like a card or ornament.
**Mess.** Cover the table, keep wipes handy and set food apart from paints and clay.

**Hot glue or scissors.** Keep tools in one place, choose a low-temperature glue gun if you use one, unplug it when you finish and take care with burns. **What makes it easier:** a mini glue gun with a low-temperature setting; follow the instructions that come with it.
**The night goes quiet.** Put on a familiar album, or ask 'what's the thing you're proudest of making?'

body.title: For the table and the room
body.dek: A mini glue gun for quick bonds, a small speaker for the playlist and acrylic paints for the pottery pieces round out the evening.

body.text: For more friend plans, see [25 girls' night ideas that aren't drinks](/journal/girls-night-ideas-that-arent-drinks), or build a standing tradition with a [mahjong night](/journal/how-to-host-a-mahjong-night) or a [book club](/journal/how-to-start-a-book-club). If someone wants to keep going solo, [junk journaling](/journal/how-to-start-junk-journaling), [embroidery](/journal/how-to-start-embroidery) or [crocheting](/journal/how-to-start-crocheting) are gentle next steps.
Settled on a project? Text the group the date and what to bring, and you're hosting.
